questions.question: What are the 8 primitive data types in Java and what are their sizes?
questions.title: 8 Primitive Data Types in Java with Sizes
questions.direct_answer: **Java has 8 primitive types**: byte (1 byte), short (2 bytes), int (4 bytes), long (8 bytes), float (4 bytes), double (8 bytes), char (2 bytes), and boolean (JVM-dependent, typically 1 bit). These are not objects — they live on the stack and hold values directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Java knowledge and whether the candidate has actually used Java or just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers confuse float/double sizes or forget that char is 2 bytes in Java (not 1 like C)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention default values (int defaults to 0, boolean to false, char to \u0000) and that primitives can't be null

sections.title: The 8 Primitive Types
Key Points
sections.content:
- Primitives are **not objects** — they live on the stack, not the heap
- Default values: `int/byte/short/long` → 0, `float/double` → 0.0, `boolean` → false, `char` → \u0000
- `long` literals need `L` suffix; `float` literals need `f` suffix
- Java's `char` is 2 bytes (Unicode), unlike C where char is 1 byte
- Primitives **cannot be null**; use wrapper classes (Integer, Boolean) when null is needed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So Java has 8 primitive types. The integer types are byte, short, int, and long — going from 1 byte up to 8 bytes. For decimals we have float and double, where double is the default. Then we have char for characters — which is 2 bytes in Java because it supports Unicode — and boolean for true/false. One thing worth mentioning is that these are not objects, they sit on the stack and they can't be null, unlike their wrapper class counterparts like Integer or Boolean.

questions.question: What is the difference between instance variables, local variables, and static variables in Java?
questions.title: Instance vs Local vs Static Variables in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Instance variables** belong to an object (heap), have default values, and each object gets its own copy. **Local variables** exist only inside a method (stack), have no default values, and must be initialized before use. **Static variables** belong to the class itself (method area), shared across all instances.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java memory model and variable scoping rules
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking local variables get default values (they don't — the compiler will error if you use an uninitialized local variable)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention where each lives in memory (stack vs heap vs method area) and thread safety implications of static variables

sections.title: Three Types of Variables
Variable Types Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Instance | Local | Static |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belongs to | Object | Method | Class |
| Memory | Heap | Stack | Method Area |
| Default value | Yes (0/null/false) | No (must init) | Yes (0/null/false) |
| Lifetime | Object lifetime | Method call | Program lifetime |
| Access | Through object | Within method only | Through class name |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So there are three kinds of variables in Java. Instance variables belong to each object — every time you create a new object, it gets its own copy, and they live on the heap. Local variables exist only inside a method — they're on the stack and gone once the method returns, and importantly the compiler won't give them default values, so you must initialize them yourself. Static variables belong to the class, not any object — there's exactly one copy shared by everyone, and you access them via the class name. A good example is a counter that tracks how many objects have been created — that would be static.

groups.heading: Instance variable
groups.text: Declared in the class body, outside any method. Each object gets its own copy. Lives on the heap for the object's lifetime. Gets a default value (0, null, false) automatically.

groups.heading: Local variable
groups.text: Declared inside a method or block. Exists only while that method runs — on the stack. No default value; the compiler forces you to initialize it before use.

groups.heading: Static variable
groups.text: Belongs to the class, not any object. One shared copy for all instances. Lives in the method area for the program's entire lifetime. Gets default values like instance variables.

items: Use instance variables for per-object state — like a user's name or salary.
Use static variables for shared state — like a counter of all objects created.
Use local variables for temporary computation within a method — they're automatically cleaned up.

beats.text: In a simple Employee class: static int count tracks total employees (shared), String name is an instance variable (each Employee has their own), and int bonus inside giveRaise() is local. Non-obvious: forgetting to initialize a local variable is a compile error, not a runtime error.

speakable_v2.cap: The big gotcha: local variables have no default — the compiler rejects uninitialized locals immediately.

questions.question: What is the var keyword in Java and when should you use it?
questions.title: var Keyword and Local Type Inference in Java 10
questions.direct_answer: **`var` is local type inference** introduced in Java 10. It lets the compiler infer the variable's type from the right-hand side expression. It can only be used for **local variables with an initializer** — not for fields, method parameters, or return types.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern Java features and understanding that var doesn't make Java dynamically typed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking var means dynamic typing like JavaScript — Java is still statically typed, the type is fixed at compile time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that var reduces boilerplate especially with generics, and explain where it cannot be used (fields, parameters, null initializer)

sections.title: var — Local Type Inference
sections.content:
```java
// Without var
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();

// With var — cleaner, same type at compile time
var names = new ArrayList<String>();

// var infers type from right side
var count = 42;          // inferred as int
var message = "hello";   // inferred as String
var pi = 3.14;           // inferred as double
```

`var` is **not** a keyword that makes types dynamic. The type is determined at compile time and never changes. It's purely a developer convenience to avoid repeating obvious type information.

**Where var CANNOT be used**:
- Class fields
- Method parameters
- Return types
- Without an initializer (`var x;` is illegal)
- With null initializer (`var x = null;` is illegal)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `var` was added in **Java 10** as JEP 286
- Only valid for **local variables** that have an initializer
- Java remains **statically typed** — var just lets the compiler infer the type
- Reduces verbosity especially with complex generic types
- Cannot be used with `null` as the initializer (compiler can't infer a type)
- The variable type is fixed after inference — you can't reassign a different type

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So `var` was introduced in Java 10 for local type inference. What it does is let the compiler figure out the type from whatever you assign on the right side — so instead of writing `ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>()` you can just write `var list = new ArrayList<String>()`. Java is still statically typed though — the type is locked in at compile time, it's not like JavaScript where the type can change. The main restriction is that var only works for local variables with an initializer, not for fields or method parameters.

questions.question: What does the final keyword do when applied to a variable in Java?
questions.title: final Variables in Java — Constants and Immutable References
questions.direct_answer: **`final` on a variable means it can only be assigned once**. For primitives, the value can't change. For object references, the reference can't point to a different object — but the object's internal state can still be mutated. It's the reference that's final, not the object itself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the distinction between a final reference and an immutable object — a classic gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking final makes an object immutable — it only prevents reassignment of the reference, not modification of the object's contents
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify the difference between final reference vs truly immutable object, and mention final instance variables must be initialized in constructor or declaration

sections.title: final Variables Explained
sections.content:
```java
final int MAX = 100;
MAX = 200;  // Compile error — can't reassign final primitive

final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("hello");   // OK — modifying the object's content
list = new ArrayList<>();  // Compile error — can't reassign the reference
```

For **primitives**: `final` makes it a constant. Once set, the value never changes.

For **object references**: `final` means the reference variable always points to the same object. But you can still call methods that change the object's state — like adding to a final List.

If you want a truly immutable object, you need to design the class to be immutable (like `String` or `LocalDate`).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `final` on a primitive = constant value (can never change)
- `final` on a reference = always points to same object (content can still change)
- `final` local variables must be assigned before use
- `final` instance variables must be initialized at declaration OR in every constructor
- Convention: final constants use ALL_CAPS with underscores (`MAX_SIZE`)
- `final` does NOT mean thread-safe by itself for object references

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So `final` on a variable means you can only assign it once — after that, any attempt to reassign it is a compile error. For primitives like int, that means the value is a constant and can never change. But for object references, it's a bit tricky — the reference can't point to a different object, but you can still modify the object itself. So a final ArrayList can still have items added to it, you just can't make that variable point to a brand new ArrayList. If you want the object to be truly immutable, you need the class itself to be immutable, like String.

questions.question: What will this code print — and why? `int a = 5; int b = a; b = 10; System.out.println(a);`
questions.title: Java Primitive Copy vs Reference Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: It prints **5**. Primitives in Java are copied by value. When `b = a` executes, `b` gets a copy of the value 5. Changing `b` to 10 has no effect on `a` — they are completely independent variables.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands pass-by-value and the difference between primitives and objects in Java
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing this with object references where two variables can point to the same object
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with object reference behavior — if a and b were both references to the same object, mutating via b would affect what a sees

sections.title: Primitives are Copied by Value
sections.content:
```java
int a = 5;
int b = a;   // b gets a COPY of the value 5
b = 10;      // only b changes
System.out.println(a);  // prints 5 — a is unchanged
```

With primitives, assignment creates an independent copy. `a` and `b` are two separate memory locations on the stack.

Contrast with objects:
```java
int[] arrA = {1, 2, 3};
int[] arrB = arrA;  // both point to SAME array
arrB[0] = 99;
System.out.println(arrA[0]);  // prints 99 — same object!
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Primitives are **value types** — assignment copies the value
- Two primitive variables are always independent
- Object references are also passed by value — but the value IS the reference (memory address)
- Java is always **pass-by-value** — but for objects, the value is a reference
- Changing a primitive variable never affects other variables

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: This prints 5. When you write `b = a` with primitives, Java copies the actual value — so b gets its own copy of 5, completely independent from a. Changing b to 10 has no effect on a at all. Now if these were object references instead of primitives, the answer might be different — because two reference variables could point to the same object, so modifying through one would affect what you see through the other. But for primitives, it's always a copy.

questions.question: What are valid variable naming conventions in Java, and what names are not allowed?
questions.title: Java Variable Naming Conventions and Rules
questions.direct_answer: **Java variable names** must start with a letter, underscore `_`, or dollar sign `$` — never a digit. They are case-sensitive, can't be reserved keywords, and by convention use **camelCase** for variables and methods. Constants use ALL_CAPS with underscores.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to Java conventions and basic language rules — separates those who've actually written Java from those who've just read about it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that $ is technically valid (though unusual), or thinking Java naming is the same as SQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the distinction between naming rules (enforced by compiler) vs naming conventions (followed by developers for readability)

sections.title: Naming Rules vs Conventions
sections.content:
**Legal names** (compiler enforced):
- Must start with: letter, `_`, or `$`
- After first char: letters, digits, `_`, `$`
- Case-sensitive (`age` and `Age` are different)
- Cannot be a reserved keyword (`int`, `class`, `return`, etc.)
- No spaces or special characters (`@`, `-`, `!`)

**Conventions** (team agreements, not enforced):
```java
int employeeAge = 25;      // camelCase for variables
String firstName = "John"; // camelCase
final int MAX_SIZE = 100;  // UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants
class EmployeeService {}   // PascalCase for classes
```

**Invalid names**: `2count`, `my-var`, `int`, `@value`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Variables, methods: **camelCase** (employeeName, calculateSalary)
- Classes, interfaces: **PascalCase** (EmployeeService, Runnable)
- Constants (static final): **UPPER_SNAKE_CASE** (MAX_RETRY_COUNT)
- Packages: **all lowercase** (com.company.service)
- Can start with `_` or `$` but this is discouraged in regular code
- Reserved words like `int`, `class`, `return` can never be variable names

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So Java has both rules and conventions for naming. The rules enforced by the compiler are: the name must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign — never a digit — and it can't be a reserved keyword like int or class. Conventions are the patterns the Java community follows: variables and methods use camelCase, classes use PascalCase, and constants use ALL_CAPS with underscores. Java is also case-sensitive, so `age` and `Age` are completely different variables. Following these conventions makes your code immediately readable to any Java developer.
